summary: Instagram is where almost all the audience is: most Hindi videos get 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 100. The best videos use a 'this sensor doesn't X, it only does Y' myth-busting hook on a familiar robot or gadget, and clap-switch and robot topics did best on both platforms. Videos with question-style titles ('Kaise kaam karta hai? 🤔') and the English Arduino video did poorly, and many were never posted to Instagram.
winningPattern: Short Hindi (Hinglish) videos about a familiar gadget or hobby robot (clap switch, line follower, gyro robot, IR sensor, DHT11) with a surprising myth-busting title: 'X doesn't do [obvious thing], it only does [real thing]' or 'without X the robot falls'. Posted to Instagram Reels first, where reach is 1,000+; YouTube only pulls 500-700 views on robot and clap-switch topics. Shares spike on relatable everyday-danger topics (UV in cloudy weather, soil sensor), and saves spike on maker-useful topics (gyro, clap switch, DHT11).
doMore: Post every video to Instagram Reels; the 10 videos with no Instagram numbers all stayed under 80 total views
Use the 'Sensor doesn't X, only does Y' myth-bust title with one emoji
Make more hobby-robot and clap-switch style videos (gyro, line follower, IR obstacle) since they work on both platforms
Add a share trigger line like 'send this to a friend who thinks...' on everyday-life topics such as sunburn, soil, health
Test one cliffhanger hook ('Without this, the robot falls') against the myth-bust style and compare saves
stopDoing: Generic 'X Kaise Kaam Karta Hai? 🤔' question titles, which averaged under 30 views
Posting English or YouTube-only videos, and near-duplicate topics like a fourth clap-switch or PIR video in a row
